topic: Domain-specific visual research: how hydrology, water-resources and climate scientists present themselves online — imagery, palettes, data-figure reuse, field photography, dataset/tool conventions, and audience needs — for satishregonda.in
key_findings: THE COMPETITIVE BASELINE IN INDIAN HYDROLOGY IS EXTREMELY LOW. Every peer site I fetched is a builder template or plain HTML: Satish's own site is Google Sites; Ankit Agarwal's HydroClimX lab (IIT Roorkee, https://www.hydroclimx.com/publications) is Google Sites with black-on-white and blue hyperlinks; Subimal Ghosh (IIT Bombay) is Wix with a visible Wix promo banner; Balaji Rajagopalan (CU Boulder, https://civil.colorado.edu/~balajir/) is unstyled ~2005 HTML with a nav of exactly Home / CV / Publications / Courses / Students. A genuinely designed, editorially crafted site would be a category-of-one in Indian hydrology — the bar is not 'beat other beautiful sites', it is 'be the only one'.

VERIFIED NWS/NOAA FLOOD-STATUS PALETTE (extracted from live water.noaa.gov page state): Major #CC33FF, Moderate #FF0000, Minor #FF9900, Action #FFFF00, No Flooding #009F0B. NWPS impact classes from map.css: .extreme #d60000, .severe #ff5454, .moderate #ff7400, .minor #ffc100, .unknown #b6b6b6. This is the single most recognizable colour convention in operational hydrology worldwide — a hydrologist reads purple as 'major flood' instantly.

VERIFIED INDIAN CONVENTIONS. CWC flood categories: Normal / Above Normal (yellow, water level ≥ Warning Level) / Severe (orange, ≥ Danger Level) / Extreme (≥ Highest Flood Level); a special 'Orange Bulletin' is issued every 3 hours in Severe situations. IMD colour-coded warnings by 24-hour rainfall: Green <64 mm, Yellow 64.5–115.5 mm, Orange 115.6–204.4 mm, Red >204.5 mm. Satish's Indian audience (GHMC, NDMA, Telangana state, journalists) already speaks this language.

THE NWS RAINBOW QPE RAMP IS A TRAP. Verified from the live NWPS page: #2BC0F5 → #3B79BB → #0C1287 → #28FA3B → #189624 → #0E5918 → #F8FA3D → #FDD469 → #F68C28 → #F50719 → #A20311 → #700209 → #F600F2 → #7240D6 → #D7D7D7 for 0.01→10+ inches of rainfall. Every hydrologist recognizes it; it is also perceptually non-uniform, non-monotonic in lightness, and fails colour-vision deficiency. Never use it decoratively.

WAGENINGEN (world #1 in water/agri research) USES A CREAM-PAPER PALETTE, NOT BLUE. Verified hexes from wur.nl: ground #F3ECD3 and #FBF6E5 (warm cream), ink #002B47 (deep navy), #153816 (near-black green), #661118 (oxblood), #88C9E4 (pale sky as accent only), #97C600 (lime), #F47C00 (orange). Cream + deep navy is the most credible 'serious water science' route that dodges the blue-gradient cliché entirely.

COPERNICUS CLIMATE (climate.copernicus.eu) leads with RED, not blue. Verified: #AF1D29 (deep red, 422 occurrences — the dominant brand colour), #273B4B (slate navy), #55BFD0 (cyan), #FAA73E (amber), #618888 (sage), #A0B128 (olive), #941333 (wine). Typeface: Lato. Proof that a climate institution can be instantly legible without being blue.

CUAHSI — the US hydrologic science consortium (https://www.cuahsi.org/) — brands in SLATE AND GREEN: #324759 slate, #3D624C forest green, #A8CCCA pale teal, #B0C7AB sage, #283947/#314E3D dark variants. The community's own umbrella body deliberately avoids the water-droplet blue.

UPSTREAM TECH'S HYDROFORECAST (https://www.upstream.tech/hydroforecast) is near-monochrome: #F0F4F7, #E9EFF4, #EBF3F6, #D5DEE2, #AEBBC5, #98A7B6, #667481, #242C31, #1E2428 — a cool-gray scale with essentially zero brand chroma, plus Lato. All colour is reserved for the hydrographs. This is the single best 'steal this' for a research site: the UI is grayscale so that every coloured pixel is data.

TYPEFACES ACTUALLY IN USE IN THIS FIELD (all verified from live CSS): NASA Earth Observatory → Public Sans Web (USWDS); CIRES → Inter; Pangeo → Inter Variable; ICIMOD → Roboto Slab + Source Sans Pro; IWMI → Source Serif 4; Utrecht Physical Geography → Open Sans + Merriweather; Our World in Data → Lato + Playfair Display; NOAA NWPS → Proxima Nova; Copernicus/Upstream → Lato; Google Flood Hub → Google Sans Flex + Roboto Mono. Note how many pair a slab/serif display with a neutral sans — the field reads slab-serif as 'scientific report', not 'startup'.

SCIENTIFIC COLOUR MAPS (Crameri) GIVE VERIFIED, DEFENSIBLE ACCENT COLOURS. I extracted 7-stop samples directly from the cmcrameri source tables. davos: #00054A #1C3F83 #43709D #6C8E93 #99AD88 #E3E7B8 #FEFEFE. lapaz: #1A0C64 #263C85 #36679D #5C8CA3 #94A298 #DAC1A8 #FEF2F3. oslo: #010101 #10263C #1F4C7B #507BBC #89A0CA #BFC5CF #FFFFFF. nuuk: #05598C #386982 #6F878D #A1A698 #BAB98D #D2D184 #FEFEB2. vik (diverging): #001261 #06548B #71A8C4 #ECE5E0 #D39774 #A94512 #590008. cork: #2C194C #2F5C8D #83A1BE #E6EDEC #8EB38D #317430 #0F2903. broc: #2C1A4C #305C8C #8BA7C2 #EBEEEC #C5C58F #70703D #262600. All are perceptually uniform, colour-vision-deficiency readable, and survive black-and-white printing.

CMOCEAN GIVES OCEANOGRAPHIC/HYDROLOGIC SEMANTICS. Verified 7-stop samples: deep #FDFECC #A5DFA7 #5DBAA4 #488E9E #3E6495 #3F396C #281A2C. dense #E6F1F1 #A2CEE2 #76A4E5 #7871D5 #7642A5 #621D62 #360E24. rain #EEEDF3 #D5C1A8 #91A77D #3D8E6E #046B6D #224359 #221B38. turbid #E9F6AB #D3C671 #BF9747 #A1703B #795338 #4D392D #221F1B. tempo #FFF6F4 #C3D1BA #7DB390 #2A937F #156D73 #1C455B #151D44. delta (diverging) #112040 #1C67A0 #6CB5B3 #FFFDCD #AAAC20 #187328 #172313. 'rain' and 'turbid' are the two most India-monsoon-appropriate ramps and neither is a blue gradient.

COLORBREWER'S BrBG IS THE CANONICAL WATER SURPLUS/DEFICIT DIVERGING SCHEME: #A6611A #DFC27D #F5F5F5 #80CDC1 #018571 (brown = dry, teal = wet). Any hydrologist reading a drought/monsoon-anomaly map expects brown-to-teal. Also verified: PuBuGn #F6EFF7 #BDC9E1 #67A9CF #1C9099 #016C59, YlGnBu #FFFFCC #A1DAB4 #41B6C4 #2C7FB8 #253494, RdYlBu #D7191C #FDAE61 #FFFFBF #ABD9E9 #2C7BB6.

NATCAP INSIGHTS (https://www.natcapinsights.com/) uses BLACK-AND-WHITE TOPOGRAPHIC CONTOUR LINE ART as a repeating structural motif — layered over dark ground, behind text, as section dividers. This is the tasteful answer to 'how do we look like water science without stock river photos': line-art cartography as texture, not photography as wallpaper.

REAL SOURCE FOR CUSTOM CARTOGRAPHIC LINE ART EXISTS AND IS FREE. HydroSHEDS HydroRIVERS (https://www.hydrosheds.org/products/hydrorivers): 8.5 million river reaches, avg 4.2 km, 35.9 million km of rivers, 15 arc-second resolution, shapefile or geodatabase, regional Asia subset available, free for scientific/educational/commercial use with attribution. Plus HydroBASINS for sub-basin polygons. Natural Earth 10m physical vectors (https://www.naturalearthdata.com/downloads/10m-physical-vectors/) is public domain. Together these let you draw a bespoke Godavari/Krishna/Musi river-network SVG that is genuinely his research area — not clip art.

IWMI'S PHOTO CREDIT AND ALT-TEXT CONVENTIONS, verified from live HTML: credit line reads 'Photo: Madeline Dahm / IWMI' or 'Photo: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo' — photographer slash institution, always visible, never hidden in a tooltip. Alt text describes the scene, not the subject matter: alt="The view from the end of a canal in the West Bank". Adopt both verbatim.

NASA EARTH OBSERVATORY'S IMAGE-STORY FORMAT (https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory) is the gold standard for a blog built around imagery: one hero image + headline + read-time estimate ('4 min read') + date + body + explicit instrument/mission credit (Aqua, EPIC, OLI). Captions do plain-language visual description first ('A V-shaped fjord cuts through barren brown land, with one patch of swirling water marked by white sea ice and another one colored turquoise by suspended sediment'), science second. Thumbnails are a fixed 720×480.

GOOGLE'S FLOOD FORECASTING PAGE (https://sites.research.google/floodforecasting/) is the field's best 'explain the model' page. Structure: silent looping hero video → 'Flood Hub' product → 'Alerts and notifications' → two 'Research breakthrough:' sections → 'Real world impact' (case-study photos of affected communities, named partners) → 'Discover more' carousel. Its centrepiece is a labelled layered technical diagram showing a hydrology model stacked with an inundation model. Diagram-as-hero, not photo-as-hero.

ALT TEXT FOR DATA FIGURES HAS A PUBLISHED 4-LEVEL MODEL (from HCI/GSA/AIP accessibility guidance): L1 construction (chart type, axis labels), L2 statistics (extremes, correlations), L3 takeaways (trends, patterns), L4 domain insight and societal context. Alt text must NOT duplicate the caption — caption and alt serve different purposes. Spell out Greek symbols and element names.

DARK-MODE HANDLING FOR PAPER FIGURES IS A SOLVED PROBLEM: apply `filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg)` via an opt-in class (e.g. `.figure-invertable`) inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, never globally, and never to photographs. Selective application prevents double-inversion.

raftwaters.in DOES NOT CURRENTLY RESOLVE — I got HTTP 000 / no DNS response on https://, http:// and www. variants. Plan the RAFT page to stand alone and degrade gracefully if the outbound link is dead at launch. (UNVERIFIED whether it is merely not yet provisioned.)

IITH'S OWN BRAND ACCENT, verified from iith.ac.in CSS: #D1402A (brick/terracotta) on a warm white #FDFBF8, with #0F172A ink. A subtle terracotta accent would tie the site to the institute without ever using the IITH logo as decoration — and terracotta/laterite is authentically Deccan.

OUR WORLD IN DATA (https://ourworldindata.org/water-access) is the strongest editorial-typography reference in this space: Lato body + Playfair Display headings, ink #1D3D63 and #002147, tints #DBE5F0 / #F0F4FA / #E7F2FF, single red accent #CE261E. 347 font-family declarations for Lato vs 92 for Playfair — the serif is used sparingly, for display only.
recommendations: DERIVE THE BRAND ACCENT FROM A STOP ON THE SCIENTIFIC COLORMAP THE SITE'S CHARTS USE. This is the intellectually honest move and it is unique: pick `davos` or `lapaz` from Crameri's Scientific Colour Maps, take the mid-dark stop (#43709D from davos, or #36679D from lapaz) as the link/accent colour, and use the full ramp for every map and hydrograph on the site. Then the accent colour is not decoration — it is literally the colour of the data. Nobody else in the field does this, it is defensible in one sentence to a hydrologist, and it guarantees CVD accessibility and black-and-white printability by construction.

GO WARM-GROUND, NOT WHITE, NOT BLUE. Recommended base: page ground #FBF7F0 (Wageningen-verified family #FBF6E5/#F3ECD3), ink #14202B (deep slate-navy, in the family of Wageningen #002B47 / OWID #1D3D63), rule/hairline #DFD6C8, muted text #5C6670. Then exactly two chromatic accents: (a) the colormap-derived water blue #43709D for links, active states and 'data' framing; (b) a laterite terracotta #C0512E — a desaturated cousin of IITH's #D1402A — for section markers, the news/blog eyebrow, and hover. Warm paper + deep ink instantly reads 'field notebook / scientific report' and structurally cannot be mistaken for a blue-gradient tech template.

MAKE THE PRIMARY VISUAL MOTIF A DRAWN RIVER NETWORK, NOT A PHOTO. Take HydroRIVERS (Asia subset) + HydroBASINS, clip to the Godavari, Krishna and Musi basins, export as hairline SVG at 0.5–1px, tint it at 6–10% opacity of the ink colour, and use it as: the hero background behind the name, a section-divider band, and the footer texture. Same geometry, three crops, three scales. This is his actual study area — it is autobiographical, it costs nothing in page weight, it scales perfectly, and it is the exact opposite of a stock river photo. Add a hairline hydrograph (a real observed-vs-forecast trace from one of his papers, redrawn as SVG) as a secondary motif for the RAFT/forecasting sections.

BUILD A FOUR-DOOR HOMEPAGE KEYED TO THE FOUR AUDIENCES. Above the fold: name, one-line identity ('Hydrology and water resources — streamflow forecasting, monsoon variability, urban flooding — IIT Hyderabad'), portrait, and four labelled entry points: 'Research', 'Publications', 'Join the group' (with a live yes/no on recruiting), 'RAFT team'. Below the fold: a 3-item news strip, a 'Currently' block (2-3 sentences he can edit weekly), and a 'Data, code & tools' strip surfacing SnapFlood / UFIS. A prospective student, a collaborator, a program officer and a journalist should each hit their target in one click.

PUT A LIVE RECRUITING STATUS BLOCK ON THE HOMEPAGE AND MAKE IT A SINGLE SHEET CELL. Prospective PhD/MTech applicants are the highest-volume audience and every peer site fails them. A boxed block reading 'Accepting PhD students for the Jan 2027 intake — apply by 15 Nov. I am especially looking for people interested in X.' with a date and an email link, driven by one row in the Google Sheet, is the highest-ROI element on the entire site. Include what alumni went on to do — Subimal Ghosh's site does this and it is the single most persuasive thing on it.

USE HIS OWN PAPER FIGURES AS THE SECTION IMAGERY, RE-RENDERED, NOT SCREENSHOTTED. Rules: (1) crop hard — take one panel, never a 6-panel figure; (2) strip the original axis furniture and re-typeset labels in the site's typeface at site scale; (3) re-colour to the site's chosen scientific colormap so every figure on the site shares one ramp; (4) export SVG where possible, 2x PNG otherwise; (5) always caption with a one-line plain-language reading plus 'From [Author et al., Year], [Journal]. CC BY 4.0.' if the paper is open access, or 'Adapted from…' with a permission note if not; (6) tag every re-rendered chart `.figure-invertable` for the dark-mode invert; (7) write 4-level alt text (chart type + axes, extremes, trend, so-what).

FIELD PHOTOGRAPHY: SHOOT FOR AN EDITORIAL SET, NOT AN ALBUM. Give him a shot list of exactly six to eight images and stop there: (1) a wide landscape of a Deccan river/reservoir at low sun; (2) hands-on-instrument close-up (gauge, sensor, notebook, drone controller); (3) students working, backs-and-shoulders, mid-task, not lined up smiling; (4) a wet, unglamorous urban-flooding street in Hyderabad; (5) a drone/aerial oblique; (6) a portrait of him in the field, not in an office. Editorial-ness comes from: consistent grade (one LUT — slightly desaturated, warm shadows, no HDR), consistent aspect ratios (use 3:2 and 16:9 only), generous negative space for text overlay, hard crops that cut people at the frame edge, and a visible credit line 'Photo: <Name> / RAFT, IIT Hyderabad' in the IWMI format. What makes it look like a slideshow: uniform centre-composition, everything shot at eye level at noon, group photos, and more than one photo per section.

ADOPT ONE PHOTO CREDIT AND ONE ALT-TEXT CONVENTION SITE-WIDE. Credit format: 'Photo: {Name} / {Affiliation}' rendered in 12px muted text directly beneath the image, always present, never a hover tooltip. Alt text describes what is visible ('Students measuring water level at a staff gauge on the Musi during the 2023 monsoon'), not the topic. Build both as required fields in whatever Sheet drives the image library, so he physically cannot publish an uncredited or undescribed image.

TYPOGRAPHY: PAIR A SLAB OR TRANSITIONAL SERIF FOR DISPLAY WITH A NEUTRAL SANS FOR TEXT, MATCHING FIELD CONVENTION. All verified available on Google Fonts (I checked, all HTTP 200): Source Serif 4 (IWMI's choice), Newsreader, Spectral, Literata, Crimson Pro, Bitter, Fraunces for display; Public Sans (NASA Earth Observatory's choice), Inter / Inter Tight (CIRES, Pangeo), Libre Franklin, Archivo, IBM Plex Sans for text; IBM Plex Mono for station IDs, DOIs, dataset names and numbers. My pick: Source Serif 4 display + Public Sans text + IBM Plex Mono for data — it is field-native, editorially warm, and none of the three reads as a startup. Use the mono deliberately for every quantity (basin areas, gauge names, lead times, DOIs) — it signals 'this person works with data' more cheaply than any graphic could.

GIVE DATASETS, CODE AND TOOLS A FIRST-CLASS SECTION WITH THE METADATA THE FIELD EXPECTS. Per item: name, one-sentence what-it-is, spatial extent, temporal coverage, resolution, format, licence, DOI (Zenodo), code repo link, associated paper, and a citation string the visitor can copy. This is what CAMELS/Caravan-era hydrologists look for and what NCAR HAP (https://ncar.github.io/hydrology/) separates into MODELS / DATASETS / PAPERS as top-level nav. SnapFlood and UFIS should each get a card here with a screenshot, the Play Store link, and a 'how to cite' line.

NOD TO OPERATIONAL COLOUR CONVENTIONS ONLY INSIDE FLOOD CONTENT, NEVER AS BRAND. If a section discusses flood severity, use the audience's own semantics: CWC's Normal / Above Normal (yellow) / Severe (orange) / Extreme, or the NWS ladder (#FFFF00 action, #FF9900 minor, #FF0000 moderate, #CC33FF major). Show it as a small labelled legend chip, which reads as domain fluency. Using those saturated colours anywhere else on the site would read as an alarm state.

USE THE NASA EARTH OBSERVATORY STRUCTURE FOR THE BLOG. Each post: one hero image (photo, map or re-rendered figure), headline, date, estimated read time, a 1-2 sentence standfirst, body, and a credit line. Fixed hero aspect ratio across all posts so the index page is a clean grid. Categories he'll actually use: Field notes, Monsoon watch, Papers explained, Group news, Teaching. Give him a 'Papers explained' template so a blog post can be generated from a paper he already wrote — that is the only way a busy professor keeps a blog alive.

MAKE THE RAFT PAGE A SINGLE SCROLLING NARRATIVE, NOT A MINI-SITE. Sequence: what RAFT is (one paragraph) → a full-bleed field photo of the team → the current people grid → three-to-four active project cards, each with a figure/map → tools (SnapFlood, UFIS) → 'Full group site → raftwaters.in' as a single prominent outbound card at the bottom. Because raftwaters.in currently does not resolve, make that card a component with a flag so the link can be hidden until the domain is live without touching the layout.

TEST THE PAGE PRINTED IN GREYSCALE AND UNDER A DEUTERANOPIA SIMULATOR BEFORE LAUNCH. Because the palette derives from Crameri maps this should pass by construction, but a program officer at DST or the World Bank genuinely may print the CV/projects page. Ensure link colour is distinguishable by more than hue (underline on hover minimum), and that every map or chart has a text alternative that carries the actual finding.

PROVIDE A ONE-CLICK PRESS KIT. Journalists spike on this site during monsoon and flood events. A '/press' page with: a 25-word bio, a 60-word bio, three approved high-res portraits (download links), his phone/email, three quotable sentences on urban flooding in Hyderabad, and a list of past media appearances. Nobody in Indian hydrology has this and it converts directly into coverage.

## 2. Proposed palette (three routes, all sourced)

**Route A — "Deccan paper" (my recommendation).** Ground `#FBF7F0`; secondary ground `#F3ECE1`; ink `#14202B`; muted `#5C6670`; hairline `#E2D9CB`; link/data accent `#43709D` (davos stop 3); hover/marker `#C0512E` (laterite, desaturated from IITH `#D1402A`); data ramp = full `davos` or `lapaz`; diverging = `vik` or ColorBrewer `BrBG`. Dark mode: ground `#141A1F`, ink `#EDE6DA`, accent lifts to `#6C8E93`/`#89A0CA`.

**Route B — "Slate & sage" (CUAHSI-adjacent, safer).** Ground `#FAFAF8`; ink `#324759`; secondary `#3D624C`; tints `#A8CCCA` / `#B0C7AB`; accent `#C0512E`. Reads institutional, less distinctive.

**Route C — "Instrument grey" (Upstream Tech).** Near-monochrome `#F0F4F7 → #1E2428` with literally zero brand chroma; all colour reserved for hydrographs and maps. Maximum restraint; risks reading cold/corporate for a personal site unless the photography carries the warmth.

## 3. How the field uses imagery — observed patterns

**Maps.** Everyone in this field expects a map, and a map is the fastest possible legibility signal. But the *good* sites use maps as **line art**, not as slippy-map embeds. NatCap Insights layers black-and-white topographic contour illustrations as background texture and section dividers. NASA EO uses full-bleed single satellite scenes with hard crops. Google Flood Hub uses a labelled layered *diagram* (hydrology model + inundation model stacked) as its explanatory hero rather than a photo. ICIMOD keeps geospatial tools (Mountain GeoPortal, Koshi Basin Information System, SERVIR-HKH) as linked resources, never embedded on the homepage — embedding a live map on a homepage is a performance and maintenance trap that none of the good sites take.

**Hydrographs.** NWPS is the reference implementation: observed line, forecast line, shaded uncertainty envelope, and horizontal flood-category bands (action/minor/moderate/major) drawn across the plot. Any hydrograph on Satish's site should carry those horizontal category bands even if simplified — it is the field's grammar.

**Satellite imagery.** NASA EO's caption convention is the model: plain-language *visual* description first, science second, instrument/mission credit always. Bhuvan (ISRO NRSC, verified live) is the Indian-audience-expected source and offers water body census, irrigation schemes, flood layers, Night Time Light 2012–2021, and an Open Data Archive with OGC services — link it from the tools section.

**Field photography.** IWMI is the best-in-class reference: documentary, professionally composed, real people doing real work (Himalayan flooding, West Bank canals, farmers in Myanmar), always credited `Photo: Name / IWMI`. CIRES uses the same register (scientists in winter gear under aurora, meandering rivers at sunrise) explicitly to "convey real-world research impact rather than abstract data visualization." Emery Lab (ecology) integrates field photography full-width with the mission statement and pairs it with leaf-texture graphics as subtle secondary elements.

## 4. Structural conventions the field expects

**Navigation vocabulary observed across sites:** Home · Research · Publications · People/Group · Teaching/Courses · Data & Code · News · Opportunities/Join · CV · Contact. NCAR HAP uses HOME / CONTRIBUTORS / PROJECTS / MODELS / DATASETS / PAPERS / NEWS — note MODELS and DATASETS as *peers* of PAPERS. Hydrosystems (UMass) uses Home / People / News / Research / Impact. Marc Bierkens's Utrecht profile splits into Profile / CV / Publications / Activities / Prizes / Media appearances / Research / Teaching — note **Media appearances** as a first-class section, which matters for a professor who gets called during monsoon season.

**People pages.** Subimal Ghosh's site (unstyled, but content-complete) is the field's most useful model: Postdocs (7) / Doctoral students (37, each with completion year, thesis topic, co-supervisor, **and current position**) / MTech students (15). The "current position" field — IIT, CSIRO, Max Planck — is the persuasive payload for prospective students. Emery Lab groups by role with candid photos. HydroClimX groups People + Alumni + Opportunities.

**Publications.** HydroClimX (Google Sites, but well-organised) splits into: Scientific Data · Journal Articles by year (2026 back to 2016) · Editor's Picks · Edited Books · Book Chapters · Conference Presentations · Scientific Blogs · Theses — with DOI links and direct Zenodo/Drive dataset access per entry. That "Scientific Data" and "Editor's Picks" split is a nice, low-cost editorial gesture. Akshata Naik's award-winning site includes **abstracts** inline; Ana Rebeka Kamšek's includes "meaningful takeaways beyond abstracts."

**Data/model/code.** Field expectation, set by the CAMELS/Caravan generation: a Zenodo DOI landing page, a GitHub repo for the processing pipeline, and an explicit statement that "the code is open source to improve transparency and reproducibility." CAMELS-DE (1582 gauges), CAMELS-CH (331 basins), CAMELS-ES (269 catchments) all follow the pattern: Zenodo record + GitHub pipeline + a paper. Reproduce the shape for SnapFlood/UFIS.

## 7. Practical rules for reusing paper figures

1. **Licence.** For CC-BY papers (EGU/HESS, Copernicus, AGU open-access, npj, Nature Comms) reuse on a personal site is permitted with attribution only — no permission request. Attribution must carry **Title, Author, Source, License** with a link to the licence deed (e.g. "CC BY 4.0"). For closed papers (Elsevier/Wiley/ASCE), author reuse of one's own figures on a personal website is usually permitted under the author agreement, but state "Adapted from …" and check the specific agreement.
2. **Crop.** One panel. Never a multi-panel plate. Never a screenshot with the journal's watermark or a caption baked in.
3. **Re-typeset.** Original figure fonts are 8pt Arial designed for a 90mm column. At web scale that is illegible. Re-render axis labels in the site typeface at site scale, or re-plot from source data.
4. **Re-colour.** One ramp across the whole site. If the paper used jet or the NWS rainbow, re-render in `davos`/`lapaz`/`vik`.
5. **Format.** SVG for anything vector. 2× PNG for raster. Never JPEG for a chart (ringing on text).
6. **Dark mode.** `.figure-invertable { }` and inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { .figure-invertable { filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg); } }`. Opt-in per figure. Never on photos, never globally, and if the page wrapper is inverted, invert images back.
7. **Alt text, 4 levels.** L1 chart type + axes; L2 extremes/correlations; L3 the trend; L4 the so-what. Do not repeat the caption. Spell out Greek letters.
8. **Caption.** One plain-language sentence saying what to look at, then the citation line.

## 8. Field photography — what makes it editorial vs. slideshow

Editorial: one image per section; consistent grade (single LUT, desaturated, warm shadows, no HDR halos); only two aspect ratios site-wide; hard crops that cut subjects at the frame edge; generous negative space where text overlays; mixed distance (one wide landscape, one hands-on-instrument macro, one mid-shot of people working); low sun; visible credit line; descriptive alt text.

Slideshow: everything centred; everything at eye level at noon; posed group photos; more than one photo per section; a carousel; inconsistent aspect ratios; captions that just say the location.

The specific Indian shot list worth building: Deccan reservoir/river at low sun (wide); staff gauge / ADCP / rain gauge close-up with hands; students mid-measurement from behind; a wet Hyderabad street during monsoon; a drone oblique of a basin or a flooded area; a portrait of him outdoors with equipment. Six images, shot in one or two field days, graded together, is enough to carry the entire site for years.

## 10. Award-winning academic sites worth a look (from the 2025 Best Personal Academic Websites Contest, fetched)

madeline-eppley.com (photography-forward, splits ongoing vs completed research — JS-only, I could not render it); phresonance.com (Tetine Sentell — praised specifically for *authentic field photography*); erikacedillo.com (best storytelling, environmental science); cecibaldoni.github.io (best interactive — a research page that unfolds narratively on scroll); megmindlin.com (best use of art/visuals); anaikowl.com (publications include abstracts, "Get to know me" affordances); kamsekar.github.io (accessibility values stated up front, publication takeaways beyond abstracts). None are hydrology; all are useful for the *editorial* register rather than the domain register.

exemplars.name: Wageningen University & Research — Hydrology and Environmental Hydraulics group (Netherlands)
exemplars.what_works: The world's leading water/agriculture university brands its hydrology group on WARM CREAM PAPER, not blue. Verified hexes from live CSS: grounds #F3ECD3 and #FBF6E5, ink #002B47 deep navy, #153816 near-black green, #661118 oxblood, with #88C9E4 pale sky used only as a tiny accent and #97C600 lime / #F47C00 orange for data. The result reads as a serious scientific publication rather than a water-utility brochure, and it is instantly distinguishable from every generic blue-gradient environmental site.
exemplars.steal_this: The cream ground + deep navy ink pairing as the site's base. #FBF7F0 ground / #14202B ink is a direct descendant. It is the single cheapest decision that guarantees the site cannot be mistaken for an AI-generated template, because templates default to pure white or a blue gradient.

exemplars.name: Upstream Tech — HydroForecast (US, commercial hydrologic forecasting)
exemplars.what_works: A near-monochrome cool-grey system with essentially zero brand chroma. Verified palette: #F0F4F7, #E9EFF4, #EBF3F6, #DEE4E9, #D5DEE2, #AEBBC5, #98A7B6, #667481, #30363C, #242C31, #1E2428, #161A1C, set in Lato. Every coloured pixel on the page is a hydrograph. This is the most disciplined hydrology design I found: the interface refuses to compete with the data.
exemplars.steal_this: The rule, not the exact greys: reserve ALL chroma for data. Chrome, nav, cards, buttons, footers stay achromatic; the only saturated colour on any page belongs to a chart, a map, or a flood-category chip. It makes a small research site look expensive and it makes every figure pop without effort.

exemplars.name: NASA Earth Observatory
exemplars.what_works: The gold standard for editorial use of scientific imagery. One hero image per story, hard-cropped, with headline + date + read-time estimate ('4 min read') + body + explicit instrument credit (Aqua, EPIC, OLI). Captions open with a plain-language VISUAL description — 'A V-shaped fjord cuts through barren brown land, with one patch of swirling water marked by white sea ice and another one colored turquoise by suspended sediment' — before any science. Fixed 720×480 thumbnails give the archive a clean grid. Typeface verified as Public Sans Web (USWDS), with DM Mono for data.
exemplars.steal_this: The image-story template for his blog, verbatim: hero + headline + date + read-time + standfirst + body + credit, with a fixed hero aspect ratio site-wide. And the caption discipline: describe what is visible before explaining what it means. Public Sans is on Google Fonts (verified) and is a free, field-native text face.

exemplars.name: NOAA National Water Prediction Service
exemplars.what_works: The operational grammar of flood communication that every hydrologist worldwide has internalised. Verified flood-status ladder from the live page state: Major #CC33FF, Moderate #FF0000, Minor #FF9900, Action #FFFF00, No Flooding #009F0B; impact classes .extreme #d60000, .severe #ff5454, .moderate #ff7400, .minor #ffc100, .unknown #b6b6b6. Its hydrographs shade horizontal flood-category bands across the plot behind observed and forecast traces.
exemplars.steal_this: Two things. (1) The horizontal category-band hydrograph as the site's secondary line-art motif — it is instantly legible as 'flood forecasting' to a hydrologist and means nothing to a template. (2) Use the flood ladder as a small labelled legend chip inside flood content only, alongside the Indian CWC equivalent (Above Normal / Severe / Extreme), as a signal of domain fluency — never as brand colour.

exemplars.name: Copernicus Climate Change Service (ECMWF, EU)
exemplars.what_works: A major climate institution whose dominant brand colour is DEEP RED (#AF1D29, 422 occurrences in the CSS), anchored by slate navy #273B4B, with #55BFD0 cyan, #FAA73E amber, #618888 sage, #A0B128 olive and #941333 wine as a genuinely distinctive secondary set. Typeface: Lato. It proves that climate authority does not require blue.
exemplars.steal_this: The permission to make the single strongest accent WARM. A laterite/terracotta accent (#C0512E, a desaturated cousin of IIT Hyderabad's own #D1402A) against a cool water-blue data ramp gives the site a memorable, geographically honest signature — Deccan red earth against monsoon water — instead of the default blue-on-blue.

exemplars.name: CUAHSI — Consortium of Universities for the Advancement of Hydrologic Science (US)
exemplars.what_works: The umbrella body of the US hydrologic science community brands in slate and green, not blue: #324759 slate, #3D624C forest, #A8CCCA pale teal, #B0C7AB sage, #283947 / #314E3D dark variants. That the field's own institution avoids water-blue is the strongest possible argument that water-blue is not required for domain legibility.
exemplars.steal_this: The slate-plus-sage pairing as a fallback palette if warm-cream is rejected. More importantly, the evidence to give the professor when he asks 'shouldn't a water site be blue?' — the answer, with receipts, is no.

exemplars.name: NatCap Insights (natural capital / conservation consultancy)
exemplars.what_works: Uses black-and-white TOPOGRAPHIC CONTOUR LINE ILLUSTRATIONS as a recurring structural motif — layered as decoration, section dividers, and visual metaphor for data-driven analysis — over a dark charcoal ground with green accents. It also segments its audience explicitly, giving government agencies, development finance institutions, universities and NGOs each a visible path.
exemplars.steal_this: Cartographic line art as texture instead of photography as wallpaper. For Satish this becomes a hairline SVG of the Godavari/Krishna/Musi river networks, generated from HydroRIVERS, tinted at 6–10% opacity, reused at three scales (hero, divider, footer). Autobiographical, weightless, infinitely scalable, and impossible for a template to produce.

exemplars.name: Google Research — Flood Forecasting / Flood Hub
exemplars.what_works: The field's best 'explain the model' page. Section sequence: silent looping hero video → Flood Hub product → Alerts and notifications → two sections literally headed 'Research breakthrough:' → 'Real world impact' with named partners and photographs of affected communities → 'Discover more' carousel of blogs, videos and papers. Its centrepiece is a labelled layered technical diagram — a global hydrology model stacked with an inundation model — used as the explanatory hero instead of a photo.
exemplars.steal_this: The diagram-as-hero pattern for the SnapFlood/UFIS page: a labelled layered graphic showing citizen reports → rainfall/hydrologic model → inundation model → alert to city agencies. One well-drawn SVG explains his flagship system faster than three paragraphs, and it is the section a journalist or a GHMC officer will screenshot.

exemplars.name: IWMI — International Water Management Institute (CGIAR)
exemplars.what_works: Best-in-class documentary water photography plus rigorous credit hygiene. Verified from live HTML: credits read 'Photo: Madeline Dahm / IWMI' and 'Photo: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo'; alt text describes the scene rather than the topic — alt="The view from the end of a canal in the West Bank". Typeface Source Serif 4; navigation organised thematically (Work / Research / Publications / Data / Where we work) rather than hierarchically.
exemplars.steal_this: The credit format 'Photo: {Name} / {Affiliation}' as a visible 12px line under every image, and the scene-describing alt-text convention. Enforce both as required fields in the Google Sheet that drives the image library so the professor cannot publish an uncredited or undescribed photo.

exemplars.name: Our World in Data — Water access
exemplars.what_works: The strongest editorial typography in the data-science space: Lato for body (347 font-family declarations) with Playfair Display used sparingly for display only (92), on an ink palette of #1D3D63 and #002147 with tints #DBE5F0 / #F0F4FA / #E7F2FF and a single red accent #CE261E. Charts and prose share one visual system; every chart carries its own source line.
exemplars.steal_this: The ratio — a display serif used at roughly a quarter the frequency of the sans, for headings only. And the practice of putting a source/citation line under every single chart, which for an academic site becomes the DOI of the paper each figure came from.

exemplars.name: NCAR Hydrometeorological Applications Program
exemplars.what_works: Puts MODELS and DATASETS in the top-level navigation as peers of PAPERS: HOME / CONTRIBUTORS / PROJECTS / MODELS / DATASETS / PAPERS / NEWS. Projects are a thumbnail grid (Hydrologic Modeling, Streamflow Forecasting, Intermediate-Complexity Downscaling). Sponsor logos (USACE, USBR, NASA, NOAA, NSF) sit in the footer as credibility signal.
exemplars.steal_this: Promoting Data & Code to top-level nav rather than burying it under Research. For Satish that section holds SnapFlood, UFIS, his R/Shiny apps and any published datasets, each with extent, coverage, resolution, format, licence, DOI, repo and a copyable citation. Plus the footer funder-logo strip — it is exactly what a program officer scans for.

exemplars.name: Emery Lab (ecology, field-science research group)
exemplars.what_works: A modular scrolling homepage that reads as a narrative rather than a directory: hero photograph + mission → 'Who We Are' → three numbered lab principles ('01. Leverage integration', '02. Prioritize curiosity', '03. Embrace the unexpected') → card-based lab news → 'Why This Work Matters' → footer. Full-width field photography carries the identity; a dark teal logo colour and subtle leaf textures do the rest. People and publications live on dedicated pages so the homepage stays clean.
exemplars.steal_this: The numbered-principles device as the 'how I work' section — three short, personally-voiced statements are the fastest antidote to a site reading as AI-generated, because they are the one thing a template cannot supply. And the discipline of keeping publications and people OFF the homepage so the homepage can be about identity.

exemplars.name: HydroClimX Lab — Ankit Agarwal, IIT Roorkee (direct Indian peer)
exemplars.what_works: Content architecture is genuinely good even though the visual design is a stock Google Sites template: publications split into Scientific Data / Journal Articles by year (2026 back to 2016) / Editor's Picks / Edited Books / Book Chapters / Conference Presentations / Scientific Blogs / Theses, each entry with full citation, DOI, and direct Zenodo or Drive links to the underlying dataset. Nav includes 'HydroClimX Café', Events, Opportunities and Gallery.
exemplars.steal_this: Two content moves: an 'Editor's Picks' / 'Selected' tier above the chronological list so a visitor sees the five papers that matter, and a dataset link attached to individual publications rather than isolated in a separate silo. Also note this is the direct competition — Google Sites — which is exactly why a designed site here is such an outsized win.

exemplars.name: Balaji Rajagopalan, CU Boulder (counter-exemplar — Satish's own PhD lineage)
exemplars.what_works: Nothing visually — it is unstyled early-2000s HTML with the nav duplicated top and bottom. But it is instructive precisely because it survives: the entire nav is Home / CV / Publications / Courses / Students, and the content is headshot, title, office/phone/fax/email, degrees 1989–1995, career 1995→present, and two lines of research interests ('Stochastic Hydrology and Hydroclimatology'; 'Understanding low frequency climate variability and its signatures on regional hydrology'). That is the field's genuine minimum viable information set.
exemplars.steal_this: The information floor — make absolutely certain the new site never loses anything on that list (office, phone, fax-equivalent, email, dated degrees, dated appointments, courses, students) in pursuit of minimalism. Minimal design, maximal facts. And note that Satish's advisor's site looking like this is the strongest possible framing for why his own should not.

pitfalls: THE BLUE GRADIENT HERO. A full-bleed blue gradient behind white text is the single most template-coded decision available and it is what every water-adjacent site defaults to. Note that Wageningen (cream + navy), CUAHSI (slate + forest green), Copernicus Climate (deep red) and Upstream Tech (achromatic grey) — all serious water/climate institutions — all avoid it.

WATER DROPLETS, WAVE DIVIDERS, RIPPLE ANIMATIONS AND FAUCET/GLOBE ICONOGRAPHY. Zero credible sites in the field use these. A hydrologist reads them as a municipal water board or a bottled-water brand. The domain-native alternatives are river networks, contour lines, basin polygons, hydrographs and staff gauges.

STOCK PHOTOS OF GENERIC RIVERS, WATERFALLS OR RAINDROPS ON GLASS. These actively destroy credibility with the peer audience because a hydrologist can tell instantly that it is not a real basin. Six real field photographs beat sixty stock images. If real photos are not available at launch, use river-network line art and no photos at all — an empty, well-set page reads as restraint; a stock photo reads as fraud.

BORROWING THE NWS QPE RAINBOW RAMP FOR DECORATION. Verified sequence: #2BC0F5 → #3B79BB → #0C1287 → #28FA3B → #189624 → #0E5918 → #F8FA3D → #FDD469 → #F68C28 → #F50719 → #A20311 → #700209 → #F600F2 → #7240D6 → #D7D7D7. It is famous, it is operational, and it is perceptually non-uniform with non-monotonic lightness and no CVD safety. Using it outside an explicitly operational context reads as a rookie error to exactly the audience he cares about.

USING FLOOD-ALERT COLOURS AS BRAND COLOURS. #FF0000 / #FF9900 / #CC33FF / #FFFF00 (NWS) and IMD's green/yellow/orange/red carry hard operational meaning to Indian and international audiences. A site that is orange all over is a site permanently reading 'Severe Flood'. Confine them to legend chips inside flood content.

EMBEDDING A LIVE SLIPPY MAP ON THE HOMEPAGE. It costs 200–500 KB of JS, breaks on slow Indian mobile connections, needs an API key that will eventually expire or start billing, and none of the good sites do it. Static SVG line art or a pre-rendered raster with a link out to the real tool.

SCREENSHOTTING PAPER FIGURES AT PUBLICATION SCALE. Journal figures are typeset at 8pt for a 90mm column. Dropped into a 1200px hero they are illegible mush with a visible watermark and a baked-in caption. Every reused figure must be re-cropped to one panel and re-typeset at web scale.

A GLOBAL filter: invert() FOR DARK MODE. It will wreck every photograph and every portrait. Inversion must be opt-in per element via a class, applied only to line art and charts, and images inside an already-inverted wrapper must be inverted back or they double-flip.

DECORATIVE alt="" ON DATA FIGURES, or alt text that just repeats the caption. Caption and alt serve different purposes and duplication gives a screen-reader user nothing. Data figures need the 4-level treatment (construction / statistics / trend / domain insight).

UNCREDITED PHOTOGRAPHY. Field photos of students, communities and flood-affected people carry ethical obligations. Every image needs a visible photographer credit, and photographs of identifiable flood-affected people need consent. IWMI and AP-syndicated credits on iwmi.org are the model. Getty results dominate searches for 'India flooding' — do NOT let a stock-licensed image slip in unlicensed.

A CAROUSEL OR SLIDESHOW ANYWHERE. TU Delft's water management page opens with a hero carousel of coastlines, landscapes, water droplets and skylines and it is the weakest thing about that page — it says nothing because it says everything. One image, chosen deliberately.

LINKING TO raftwaters.in BEFORE IT RESOLVES. As of this research the domain returns no DNS/HTTP response on https://, http:// and www variants. A dead outbound link on the flagship group page is worse than no link. Gate it behind a flag.

BURYING SNAPFLOOD THREE CLICKS DEEP, as the current site does (Research → SnapFlood). It is his most public-facing, most fundable, most quotable artefact — a citizen flood-reporting app on the Play Store feeding a city flood information system — and it is exactly what a journalist, a GHMC officer or a DST program officer arrives looking for.

HIDING THE NOAA / WORLD BANK / JOHNS HOPKINS / CU BOULDER TRAJECTORY IN PROSE. It is a genuinely rare CV for an Indian faculty member and it is currently a sentence in a paragraph. It should be a compact scannable strip.

OMITTING RECRUITING STATUS OR LETTING IT GO STALE. A block that says 'Accepting students for Jan 2026' in September 2027 is worse than no block, because it tells every prospective applicant the site is abandoned. Drive it from one Sheet cell with a review date.

A FONT PAIRING THAT READS AS SAAS. Inter + Inter, or a geometric sans display over a neutral sans body, will make the site look like a startup landing page no matter how good the content is. The field's own register is slab/transitional serif display + neutral sans text (ICIMOD: Roboto Slab + Source Sans Pro; IWMI: Source Serif 4; Utrecht: Merriweather + Open Sans; OWID: Playfair + Lato).

MORE THAN THREE TYPEFACES OR MORE THAN TWO CHROMATIC ACCENTS. With a warm ground, one water blue and one terracotta, plus a scientific ramp for data, the system is complete. A fourth colour will arrive as a 'category tag' and will be the thing that makes it look generated.

OVER-MINIMALISING AWAY THE FACTS. Balaji Rajagopalan's ugly site still lists office, phone, fax, email, dated degrees and dated appointments; Subimal Ghosh's ugly site lists 37 doctoral students with thesis topics, co-supervisors and current positions. Do not let an editorial redesign delete the information the audience actually came for. Minimal design, maximal facts.
